title: What Is Fleet Management? A Practical Guide for East African Businesses
seo_title: What Is Fleet Management? A Guide for East African Businesses
seo_desc: Fleet management explained simply: what it covers, why it matters, and how businesses in Uganda and Kenya use it to cut costs and improve safety.
excerpt: Fleet management is how a business keeps its vehicles, drivers and fuel under control. Here is what it covers, who needs it and how East African fleets get started.
content:
If your business runs more than a handful of vehicles, you are already doing fleet management. You decide who drives which vehicle, you pay for fuel and repairs, you chase drivers on the phone to find out where they are, and you deal with the fallout when something goes wrong on the road. The only question is whether you are doing it with guesswork and paperwork, or with data.

This guide explains what fleet management actually includes, why it matters so much for businesses operating in Uganda, Kenya and the wider region, and how to tell when it is time to put a proper system in place.

What does fleet management include?

Fleet management is the work of keeping a group of vehicles and drivers safe, productive and affordable to run. In practice it breaks down into five areas.

  • Tracking. Knowing where every vehicle is, where it has been and whether it is being used for the job it was assigned to. This is the foundation everything else is built on. GPS vehicle tracking gives you live location, trip history and utilisation reports instead of phone calls.
  • Maintenance. Servicing vehicles on schedule, catching faults early and keeping records of every repair. A vehicle that breaks down on the Masaka road costs far more than the service it missed. See preventive fleet maintenance.
  • Compliance. Making sure drivers respect speed limits, rest periods and company safety rules, and that vehicles carry valid licences and inspections. For oil and gas, cargo and public-sector fleets, compliance is often a contractual requirement. See fleet compliance management.
  • Driver safety. Identifying risky behaviour such as speeding, harsh braking, fatigue and phone use, and coaching drivers before it turns into an accident. AI dash cameras make this measurable.
  • Fuel. Fuel is one of the largest costs of running any fleet. Fuel management means knowing how much each vehicle consumes, spotting refills or drains that do not add up, and reducing waste from idling and aggressive driving. See fleet fuel management.

A modern fleet management system brings all five into one platform, so a manager in Kampala or Nairobi can see the whole operation on one screen rather than in five spreadsheets.

Why fleet management matters for East African businesses

The basic ideas are the same everywhere, but operating conditions in East Africa make them more pressing.

Fuel is expensive and easy to lose. Fuel is a large share of operating costs for most fleets, and siphoning, inflated refuelling receipts and unauthorised trips are common problems. Without data, losses are almost impossible to prove.

Roads are hard on vehicles. Long distances, rough surfaces and heavy loads accelerate wear. Preventive maintenance based on real mileage and engine data is far cheaper than repairing a breakdown far from the nearest workshop.

Road safety is a real business risk. An accident means injured staff, damaged vehicles, lost cargo, insurance claims and reputational damage. Monitoring driver behaviour is one of the most direct ways to reduce that risk.

Operations cross borders and remote areas. Trucks move goods along the Northern Corridor from Mombasa through Kenya and Uganda into Rwanda, South Sudan and the DRC. NGOs and oil and gas operators work far from reliable cellular coverage. Knowing where vehicles and people are is a safety issue as much as an efficiency one.

Clients and regulators expect evidence. Oil and gas operators, donors, government agencies and revenue authorities increasingly ask for trip records, driver hours and incident reports. A system produces these automatically.

Common signs you need a fleet management system

You probably need one if any of these sound familiar:

  • You find out where a vehicle is by calling the driver.
  • Fuel spend keeps rising and you cannot explain why.
  • Vehicles are used after hours or for trips you did not authorise.
  • Services are missed because nobody tracked the mileage.
  • You have had accidents, and no reliable record of what happened.
  • A client or donor has asked for trip or driver reports you cannot produce.
  • Preparing monthly fleet reports takes days of manual work.

What does it take to get started?

Getting started is simpler than many businesses expect. A typical rollout looks like this:

  1. Agree what you want to fix first. Fuel loss, unauthorised use, safety and compliance call for slightly different hardware and reports.
  2. Choose the hardware. A GPS tracker is the starting point. Depending on your goals you might add fuel level sensors, AI dash cameras, driver ID readers or temperature sensors. Our hardware range covers each of these.
  3. Install and connect. Smartwatch plug-and-play trackers are delivered to you and activated with a QR code, with no technician required. For fleets that cannot take vehicles off the road, the OnTrack app tracks vehicles from a driver's phone with no hardware installation at all.
  4. Set your rules. Speed limits, geofences, working hours and alert recipients, so the system flags exceptions instead of you hunting for them.
  5. Review and act. The value comes from using the reports: coaching drivers, scheduling services and following up on fuel exceptions.

Costs depend on fleet size, the hardware you choose and the features you need, which is why most providers quote per vehicle after understanding your operation. Talk to our team for a quote based on your fleet.

title: How to Choose a Fleet Management System in Uganda: A Buyer's Guide
seo_title: How to Choose a Fleet Management System in Uganda
seo_desc: A practical checklist for choosing a fleet management system in Uganda: the questions to ask vendors, hardware built for local roads, support and pricing.
excerpt: Choosing a fleet management system in Uganda is about more than a map on a screen. Use this checklist to compare vendors on hardware, local support, reporting and pricing.
content:
There is no shortage of companies offering vehicle tracking in Uganda. Some sell a tracker and a login. Others offer a full fleet management platform with local installation, support and reporting. On a sales call they can sound very similar, and the differences often only show up months later, when a device fails upcountry or the reports you need do not exist.

This guide sets out what to look for, and the questions to ask any vendor before you sign.

Start with the problem you want to solve

Before comparing vendors, write down the two or three problems that matter most to you. For example:

  • Fuel spend that keeps rising without explanation
  • Vehicles used for private trips or after hours
  • Accidents and risky driving
  • Missed services and unexpected breakdowns
  • A client, donor or regulator asking for trip and driver reports

Each problem points to particular features and hardware. Fuel loss needs fuel sensors or CANbus fuel data, not just GPS. Driver safety needs driver behaviour monitoring and possibly AI dash cameras. Being clear up front stops you paying for features you will not use, and stops you buying a basic tracker when you needed a full system.

Questions to ask any vendor

Use these questions in every conversation, and compare the answers side by side.

About the company

  • How long have you operated in Uganda, and who are some of your current clients in my industry?
  • Do you have a local office and local technicians, or is support handled from abroad?
  • What are your support hours, and how do I reach you in an emergency?

About the platform

  • Can I see live location, trip history, driver behaviour, fuel and maintenance in one system?
  • Which reports come as standard, and can they be scheduled to arrive automatically?
  • Is there a mobile app for managers and a separate one for drivers?
  • Can the data be exported or connected to our own systems through an API?

About the hardware

  • Which devices do you install, and where are they made?
  • What connectivity do they use, and what happens when a vehicle drives out of coverage?
  • How do you detect tampering, such as a disconnected device or signal jamming?

About the contract

  • What is included in the monthly fee, and what costs extra?
  • Who owns the hardware, and what happens to it if we cancel?
  • How long is the minimum term?

Hardware built for local conditions

Uganda's roads are hard on electronics. Dust, heat, vibration and water crossings all take their toll, and a device that works well in a European city can struggle on a murram road in the north. Look for:

  • Rugged, IP-rated housings that resist dust and water.
  • Reliable positioning. A good GNSS module and the option of an external antenna when the tracker must be hidden under metal.
  • Tamper alerts for power disconnection, antenna removal and GSM jamming.
  • Data storage so trips recorded out of coverage are uploaded once the vehicle reconnects.
  • Expandability. Fuel sensors, driver ID readers, temperature sensors and cameras should connect to the same platform.

Smartwatch trackers use 4G (GSM) connectivity with a premium GPS module in dust and water resistant housings, and connect to a full range of accessories and sensors.

Local support versus remote-only providers

When a tracker stops reporting, a vehicle is stolen or a report looks wrong, you need someone who answers quickly and can send a technician if needed. Remote-only providers can be cheaper on paper but slow to respond in practice. Ask where the nearest technician is, how quickly they can reach your depots, and whether support runs outside office hours.

Pricing models to understand

Most fleet management pricing is made up of three parts:

  • Hardware, bought outright or included in the subscription
  • Installation, sometimes free for plug-and-play devices
  • A monthly subscription per vehicle, covering platform access, data and support

The cheapest per-vehicle price is rarely the cheapest option overall. Factor in the cost of failed devices, missing reports, slow support and the fuel or vehicles you could have saved. A useful exercise is to estimate what one month of fuel loss or one avoidable breakdown costs your business and compare it with the subscription.

A simple scoring approach

Score each vendor from one to five on: fit with your main problems, hardware quality, local support, reporting, ease of use, and total cost over three years. Ask for a live demo using realistic scenarios from your own fleet, and speak to at least one existing client in a similar industry.

title: How GPS Vehicle Tracking Works (And Why It Matters for Your Fleet)
seo_title: How GPS Vehicle Tracking Works: A Guide for Fleets
seo_desc: A plain-language explanation of how GPS vehicle tracking works, what data you actually get, and the real business benefits for fleets in Uganda and Kenya.
excerpt: A plain-language look at how GPS vehicle tracking works, from the device in the vehicle to the dashboard on your screen, and what fleets actually do with the data.
content:
GPS vehicle tracking is the foundation of almost every fleet management system. Yet many fleet owners are not quite sure how it works, what data it produces or how reliable it is on East African roads. This article explains it in plain language.

The basics: device, satellites, network and dashboard

A GPS tracking system has four parts.

1. The tracking device. A small unit installed in the vehicle, wired to its power supply or plugged into its diagnostic port. Inside are a satellite positioning receiver, a mobile network modem, a motion sensor and a small backup battery.

2. The satellites. The device calculates its own position by listening to signals from navigation satellites. GPS is the American system. Many modern trackers also use other constellations such as GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou, which improves accuracy and coverage. Together these are known as GNSS.

3. The mobile network. Every few seconds or minutes, the device sends its position, speed, heading and status over the mobile network (GSM, 3G or 4G) to a server. If the vehicle is out of coverage, a good tracker stores the data and uploads it when the signal returns, so there are no gaps in trip history.

4. The platform. The server turns raw readings into something useful: a live map, trip history, reports and alerts that managers can open on a computer or phone.

The satellites only tell the device where it is. It is the mobile network and the platform that let you see it.

What data you actually get

A basic tracker gives you:

  • Live location of every vehicle on a map
  • Trip history, so you can replay any journey with start and stop times
  • Speed and speeding events
  • Ignition on and off, idling time and working hours
  • Mileage for each vehicle

Connect the tracker to the vehicle's CANbus or add sensors and accessories, and you can also see:

  • Fuel level, consumption and sudden drops
  • Engine diagnostics such as battery voltage
  • Harsh braking, acceleration and cornering
  • Which driver is behind the wheel, using an RFID card
  • Cargo temperature for refrigerated trucks
  • Door or lock status for cargo security

Real-world uses

Theft recovery and prevention. If a vehicle is stolen, live tracking shows where it is going. With an engine block relay, it can be immobilised remotely from the platform or by SMS.

Stopping unauthorised use. Geofences are virtual boundaries drawn on a map. You can be alerted when a vehicle leaves an approved area, enters a restricted one or moves outside working hours.

Proving what happened. Trip history settles disputes about delivery times, routes taken and hours worked, with clients and with drivers.

Better routing and dispatch. Knowing where every vehicle is lets dispatchers send the nearest one to the next job instead of guessing.

Fuel control. Comparing distance driven with fuel bought or used is the first step to spotting fuel loss. See our guide to fuel monitoring.

Maintenance based on real use. Mileage and engine hours trigger service reminders automatically. See preventive maintenance.

How reliable is tracking on African roads?

Accuracy is usually within a few metres in open areas, and multi-GNSS devices perform better in towns and valleys. The bigger practical issues are coverage, tampering and installation quality:

  • Coverage. Store-and-forward means trips through coverage gaps are still recorded. For operations far beyond any cellular network, such as some NGO and oil and gas work, satellite communication options are available. See satellite tracking for NGOs.
  • Tampering. Good systems alert you when the device loses power, its antenna is disconnected or the GSM signal is jammed.
  • Installation. A well-hidden, properly wired device is much harder to interfere with. An external antenna helps when the tracker must sit under metal.

GPS tracking or telematics?

GPS tracking tells you where a vehicle is. Telematics adds how it is being driven and how it is performing, using data from the engine, sensors and cameras. Most businesses start with tracking and add telematics features as their needs grow. Smartwatch FM supports both on one platform.

Getting started

Smartwatch plug-and-play trackers are delivered to you and activated with a QR code, using 4G (GSM) connectivity and a premium GPS module in a dust and water resistant housing. For fleets that cannot take vehicles off the road, the OnTrack app tracks vehicles from a phone with no hardware at all.

title: How Dash Cameras Reduce Accidents and Insurance Costs
seo_title: How Dash Cameras Reduce Accidents and Insurance Costs
seo_desc: How AI-powered dash cameras improve driver safety, cut accident risk and help lower fleet insurance costs, and what to look for in a dash cam system.
excerpt: AI dash cameras do more than record crashes. They warn drivers in real time, give managers evidence for coaching, and help fleets build a case for lower insurance costs.
content:
For years, fleet cameras were simple recorders. They captured footage that someone might review after an accident, if the memory card had not been overwritten. Modern AI dash cameras are different. They watch for risky behaviour as it happens, warn the driver in the cab, and alert the fleet manager. That shift, from recording accidents to preventing them, is why dash cameras have become one of the most effective safety investments a fleet can make.

What AI dash cams actually detect

A typical fleet system combines a road-facing camera, a driver-facing camera and a mobile digital video recorder (MDVR) linked to the tracking platform. The AI looks for events such as:

  • Fatigue: eyes closing, yawning, head nodding
  • Distraction: looking away from the road for too long
  • Phone use while driving
  • Smoking in the cab
  • No seat belt
  • Speeding, harsh braking and harsh acceleration, using tracking and motion data

When an event is detected, the driver gets an immediate in-cab warning, such as an audible alert or seat vibration for fatigue. A short video clip of the event is sent to the platform so a manager can review exactly what happened.

How cameras reduce accidents

Real-time warnings change behaviour in the moment. A fatigue alert can wake a drowsy driver before they drift off the road. A speed warning before the limit is exceeded prompts the driver to ease off.

Drivers drive differently when they know they are coached, not just watched. Over time, the number of alerts tends to fall as drivers adjust their habits.

Coaching is based on evidence. Instead of general safety talks, managers can sit down with a driver and review specific clips. Good systems let you prioritise the most serious events so supervisors are not buried in footage.

Patterns become visible. Event data shows which drivers, routes and times of day carry the most risk, so you can act where it matters most, for example by changing schedules on routes with frequent fatigue events.

The insurance cost connection

Insurance costs for a fleet are driven by claims history and perceived risk. Dash cameras can help on both sides.

  • Fewer and less severe incidents mean fewer claims over time.
  • Video evidence helps establish what really happened. When another road user is at fault, footage can protect your driver and your claims record.
  • Faster claims handling, because the facts are clear from the start.
  • A demonstrable safety programme. Driver scores and incident trends give you something concrete to show your insurer at renewal.

Whether your premium actually falls depends on your insurer and your results, so it is worth talking to your broker about how they treat telematics and camera data before you install. Some insurers in the region already work with telematics providers. Learn more about telematics for insurance.

Driver coaching, not just surveillance

Drivers are understandably wary of cameras. How you introduce them makes a big difference:

  • Explain the purpose: safety and protecting drivers from false accusations.
  • Be clear about what is recorded, who can see it and how long footage is kept.
  • Use footage to coach and recognise good driving, not only to punish.
  • Share driver scores so drivers can see their own improvement.

Fleets that frame cameras as a tool that protects drivers usually see better acceptance and better results.

What to look for in a dash cam system

  • Accurate AI detection with few false alarms, so drivers trust the warnings
  • In-cab alerts that reach the driver in real time
  • Integration with your tracking platform, so video, location and speed are in one place
  • Multi-channel recording for larger vehicles and buses
  • Prioritised event review so managers see the clips that matter
  • Robust hardware that handles heat, dust and vibration
  • Local installation and support

Dash cameras for buses and public transport

For bus operators, the same platform can add passenger information, people counting, dispatch and ticketing, giving a complete picture of each journey. See our bus and public transport solution.

title: Fuel Monitoring Systems: How They Work and What They Save You
seo_title: Fuel Monitoring Systems: How They Work and What They Save
seo_desc: How fuel monitoring systems detect fuel theft and waste, how fuel sensors and CANbus data work, and where fleets in Uganda and Kenya find real savings.
excerpt: Fuel is one of the biggest costs in any fleet, and one of the easiest to lose. This guide explains how fuel monitoring works and where the savings come from.
content:
Ask any fleet owner in Uganda or Kenya about their biggest cost and fuel will be at or near the top of the list. Ask how much of that fuel actually goes into moving the business forward, and most cannot say for certain. Fuel siphoning, inflated refill receipts, unauthorised trips, excessive idling and aggressive driving all add up, and without data they are almost invisible.

A fuel monitoring system makes them visible. Here is how it works.

How fuel data is captured

There are two main ways to measure fuel in a vehicle.

1. From the vehicle's own computer (CANbus). Newer vehicles and trucks already measure fuel level and consumption. A telematics device connected to the CANbus can read this data accurately, without drilling the tank.

2. With a fuel level sensor. Older vehicles often do not provide reliable fuel data, so a dedicated sensor is fitted in the tank. Capacitive probe sensors measure the fuel level continuously. Wireless, battery-powered sensors are also available. Smartwatch's wireless fuel level sensor runs for 5 to 10 years on its battery and avoids extra wiring.

The fuel data is sent to the platform along with the vehicle's location, speed and ignition status, so every change in fuel level is tied to a time and a place.

What the platform shows you

  • Fuel level in each tank over time
  • Consumption per trip, day or month
  • Average consumption, for example kilometres per litre
  • Refills, with the time, location and volume added
  • Drains, sudden drops that do not match driving

Alerts can be sent the moment an abnormal drop is detected, so you can respond while it is happening rather than at month end.

Common fuel loss patterns

Siphoning. Fuel drained from the tank, often at night or at a regular stop. Shows up as a sudden drop while the vehicle is stationary.

Refuelling fraud. A receipt says 200 litres were bought, but the sensor shows a smaller increase. Comparing refill data with fuel card or receipt records exposes the gap.

Unauthorised trips. Fuel used for private errands or side jobs. Trip history and working-hours rules reveal journeys that should not have happened.

Idling. Engines left running while waiting, loading or resting. Idling burns fuel while moving nowhere, and it adds up quickly across a fleet.

Driving style. Harsh acceleration, overspeeding and high engine revs all increase consumption, as well as wear on tyres and brakes.

Where the savings come from

Savings vary widely depending on how much loss and waste a fleet has to start with, so be wary of anyone who promises a fixed percentage before seeing your data. In practice, fleets save in three ways:

  • Stopping theft and fraud. Often the fastest win, because drains and short refills become obvious.
  • Reducing waste. Cutting idling and unauthorised use.
  • Improving driving. Coaching drivers on smoother driving lowers consumption over time.

Smartwatch fleet fuel management can help fleets save up to 40% on fuel, depending on where they start. The first step is to measure your own baseline for a few weeks, then track how it changes as you act on the alerts and reports.

Pairing fuel data with driver behaviour

Fuel data tells you that something happened. Driver behaviour data helps explain why. Combining the two lets you:

  • Compare consumption between drivers on similar vehicles and routes
  • Identify top and bottom performers
  • Show each driver how their habits affect fuel use
  • Recognise and reward the most efficient drivers

Our Eco-Drive solution monitors more than 90 parameters, from idling and overspeeding to harsh braking and fuel wasted, and an in-cab Eco panel can give drivers real-time feedback.

Beyond vehicles

Fuel sensors also work on stationary tanks, generators and other equipment. For businesses running generators at remote sites, fuel monitoring is an effective way to control diesel use. See remote site and generator monitoring.

Start measuring your fuel

Smartwatch captures fuel data from the CANbus on newer vehicles and fits reliable fuel sensors on older ones, with real-time alerts for refills and drains and reports for every vehicle and driver.

title: Fleet Management for Oil & Gas: Compliance, Safety and Cost Control
seo_title: Oil & Gas Fleet Management in East Africa: IVMS & Safety
seo_desc: How fleet management and IVMS help oil and gas operators and contractors in East Africa manage driving hours, improve land transport safety and control costs.
keyword: oil and gas fleet management East Africa
excerpt: Oil and gas projects hold their contractors to strict land transport safety standards. Here is how IVMS and fleet management help meet them while controlling cost.
content:
Land transport is one of the biggest safety risks in the oil and gas industry. Vehicles move people, equipment and materials over long distances, often on rough roads, in remote areas and at all hours. As oil and gas development has grown across East Africa, from the Albertine region in Uganda to projects in Kenya, Tanzania and beyond, operators have brought international land transport safety standards with them, and expect their contractors to meet them.

For transport companies and service providers, that means fleet management is no longer optional. It is a condition of doing business.

Why oil and gas fleets need specialised management

Oil and gas operations combine several risk factors at once:

  • Long journeys and long shifts, which raise the risk of fatigue
  • Remote locations with limited mobile coverage and emergency services far away
  • Heavy and hazardous loads
  • Mixed traffic on public roads shared with pedestrians, boda bodas and livestock
  • Many contractors whose drivers must all meet the same standard

Operators manage these risks through journey management, driver training and, increasingly, In-Vehicle Monitoring Systems (IVMS). International guidance such as the IOGP land transport safety recommended practice has made IVMS a common contractual requirement on oil and gas projects.

What an IVMS does

An IVMS is a telematics system configured for land transport safety. It typically records:

  • Location and route, to confirm journeys follow the approved journey plan
  • Speed and overspeeding, often against different limits for highways, towns and site roads
  • Harsh braking, acceleration and cornering
  • Driving and rest hours, against the project's driving-hours rules
  • Seat belt use
  • Driver identity, using RFID cards or other driver ID methods
  • Night driving, where it is restricted

The data is used to score drivers, report to the client and target coaching where it is needed most.

Driving hours compliance explained

Fatigue is one of the leading causes of serious road incidents. Most oil and gas projects set limits on continuous driving time, total daily driving hours and minimum rest periods. Paper logbooks are easy to falsify and hard to audit.

An electronic logging solution records each driver's hours automatically, based on ignition and movement data linked to the driver's ID. Supervisors can see who is approaching their limit, and reports show compliance across the whole fleet. Smartwatch built its driving-hours logging specifically because of the demands of the oil and gas sector.

Safety on remote sites

On remote sites, supervisors cannot see what is happening on the road. Telematics gives them eyes and ears on the ground:

  • Real-time alerts for speeding, harsh driving and fatigue
  • AI dash cameras that detect fatigue, phone use and distraction, warning the driver with an alert or seat vibration
  • Driver scoring and targeted training for the drivers who need it
  • Location of every vehicle, which matters in an emergency
  • Satellite communication options where there is no cellular network

Reporting for operators and stakeholders

Oil and gas clients expect regular, consistent reporting. A central platform can produce daily, weekly or monthly reports on the metrics that matter to the project: speeding events per 100 km, driving-hours violations, seat belt compliance, driver scores and incident trends. Automated reports save supervisors hours of manual work and make audits far easier.

Cost control

Safety and cost go together. The same data that improves safety also helps control costs:

  • Fuel monitoring detects drains and unexplained consumption, with alerts when fuel levels change abnormally
  • Idling reports show where engines are left running, cutting fuel use and CO2 emissions
  • Maintenance alerts catch faults early, before a breakdown on a remote road
  • Utilisation reports show whether vehicles are needed or sitting idle

Choosing an IVMS provider

Look for a provider that can show experience on oil and gas projects, meets your client's IVMS specification, offers driver ID and dash camera integration, provides 24/7 support, and has technicians who can reach your sites.

title: Fleet Management for NGOs: Balancing Safety, Cost and Accountability
seo_title: NGO Fleet Management in East Africa: Safety & Accountability
seo_desc: How NGOs in East Africa use fleet tracking to keep field teams safe, control costs and meet donor and audit reporting, even beyond cellular coverage.
excerpt: NGOs need their vehicles to be safe, affordable and fully accountable. Here is how fleet tracking helps humanitarian and development organisations do all three.
content:
For NGOs, vehicles are lifelines. They carry staff to remote communities, deliver supplies and support programmes across large areas. They are also a major cost, a significant safety risk and an asset that donors and auditors expect to be fully accounted for. Fleet management helps NGOs balance all three.

Donor accountability and reporting

Every shilling and dollar of donor funding must be justified. Vehicles are one of the most visible costs in a programme budget, and auditors expect clear records of how they are used.

A fleet management system provides:

  • Trip logs showing where each vehicle went, when and for how long
  • Mileage and utilisation reports per vehicle, project or cost centre
  • Fuel records that tie consumption to actual journeys
  • Evidence of authorised use, with alerts for trips outside working hours or outside approved areas

These reports are generated automatically, so programme and finance teams are not rebuilding logbooks before every audit or donor report.

Staff safety in remote and high-risk areas

Duty of care is a serious responsibility for NGOs. Field staff travel long distances, sometimes through insecure areas or regions with poor roads and limited emergency services. Knowing where vehicles are, and being alerted when something goes wrong, can be critical.

Fleet tracking supports staff safety with:

  • Live location of every vehicle, visible to the security or logistics focal point
  • Geofences that alert when a vehicle enters a restricted area or leaves an approved route
  • Driving event notifications for speeding and harsh driving
  • Driver ID, so you know who is driving each vehicle
  • Driving-hours monitoring to reduce fatigue risk on long journeys

Combined with your journey management procedures, this gives security teams the information they need to respond quickly.

Satellite tracking where cellular coverage fails

Many NGO operations take place where mobile networks are weak or absent. Standard trackers store data and upload it when coverage returns, which is fine for reporting but not for real-time safety. For truly remote operations, satellite-capable tracking keeps vehicles visible beyond the reach of cellular networks. A mix often works best: standard GSM trackers for urban and peri-urban vehicles, and satellite options for vehicles operating in remote areas.

Cost control on tight budgets

NGO budgets are tight, and every saving goes back into programmes. Fleet data helps by:

  • Reducing fuel loss through consumption reports and alerts for unusual fuel drops
  • Cutting unauthorised use, including private trips and after-hours movement
  • Lowering maintenance costs with service reminders based on real mileage
  • Right-sizing the fleet, by showing which vehicles are underused
  • Encouraging better driving, which reduces fuel use, wear and accident costs

No-hardware options for short projects

Not every project justifies installing hardware, especially for short-term or hired vehicles. App-based tracking such as Smartwatch OnTrack uses the driver's phone to track vehicles in real time and monitor driving behaviour, with no installation and no vehicle downtime.

Getting started

A sensible approach for most NGOs:

  1. Agree what matters most: safety, accountability, cost, or all three.
  2. Identify which vehicles operate in remote or high-risk areas.
  3. Choose hardware accordingly, including satellite options where needed.
  4. Set geofences, driving rules and alert recipients.
  5. Schedule the reports donors and auditors need.

title: What Is Electronic Cargo Tracking? A Guide for Transporters in Uganda and Kenya
seo_title: What Is Electronic Cargo Tracking? ECTS & RECTS Explained
seo_desc: Electronic cargo tracking explained: how e-seals secure transit cargo in East Africa, what RECTS means for transporters, and what to expect from installation.
excerpt: Electronic cargo tracking keeps transit goods sealed and visible from port to destination. Here is how e-seals work and what the regional system means for transporters.
content:
Every day, thousands of trucks carry goods in transit across East Africa, from the port of Mombasa through Kenya and Uganda to Rwanda, South Sudan, the DRC and beyond. Revenue authorities need to know that goods declared as transit actually leave the country rather than being diverted and sold without duty. Transporters need to move quickly without being stopped at every checkpoint. Electronic cargo tracking serves both.

What is electronic cargo tracking?

An electronic cargo tracking system (ECTS) uses an electronic seal or lock fitted to a container or truck, combined with GPS tracking and a central monitoring centre. From the moment cargo is sealed to the moment it reaches its destination, the system records:

  • Where the cargo is, in real time
  • Whether the seal is intact, and any attempt to tamper with it
  • Whether the truck is following its approved route, and how long it stops

If the seal is opened in the wrong place, the truck leaves its route or the device is tampered with, alerts go to the monitoring centre so authorities and the transporter can respond.

How electronic seals and locks work

An electronic seal combines a locking mechanism with tracking electronics. Typical features include:

  • Multi-GNSS positioning using GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou for accurate location
  • Tamper detection that reports any attempt to cut or open the seal
  • Controlled opening, so the container can only be opened at the right location, with the right electronic key and within the right time window
  • Long battery life for long journeys and border delays. The Smartwatch e-Seal has a 20,000 mAh battery for around 60 days of operation
  • Rugged housing rated against dust and water

For larger consignments, a primary e-Lock can control several secondary locks over Bluetooth. The Smartwatch primary e-Lock controls up to seven secondary locks, so a whole consignment is opened or kept sealed together.

The regional context: RECTS

To reduce delays on the Northern Corridor, the revenue authorities of East African Community partner states introduced the Regional Electronic Cargo Tracking System (RECTS). Instead of fitting a new seal at each border, one seal can follow the cargo across participating countries, with authorities sharing monitoring data. This supports the EAC Single Customs Territory and cuts the time and cost of transit.

For transporters, this generally means working with an approved RECTS vendor, having seals fitted and monitored by that vendor, and following the procedures of the revenue authorities in each country. Requirements, approved vendors and fees are set by the authorities and can change, so always confirm the current rules with the Uganda Revenue Authority, the Kenya Revenue Authority or your clearing agent before you move cargo.

Smartwatch Solutions is a KRA-approved vendor for EAC RECTS, with regional support offices in Nairobi, Kampala and Mombasa and a 24/7 Centralised Monitoring Centre.

Benefits beyond compliance

Better cargo security. Goods stay sealed and accounted for throughout the journey, which reduces theft and pilferage.

Faster clearance. Real-time data on cargo location and status supports quicker inspection and clearance at border posts and inland bonded warehouses.

Visibility for your customers. You can share tracking data with cargo owners and give accurate arrival times.

Lower insurance and loss costs as theft and disputes fall.

Fuel tanker monitoring. For liquid cargo, compartment monitoring with flow meters can measure fuel volume in each compartment of a tanker, flagging losses in transit.

What to expect during installation

  1. Registration with the vendor and confirmation of your vehicles and routes.
  2. Seal fitting at the loading point or designated location, linked to the customs declaration.
  3. Live monitoring throughout the journey by the monitoring centre.
  4. Seal removal at the destination, bonded warehouse or exit point, once authorised.
  5. Reporting, with a full record of the journey available to you and the authorities.

Talk to an approved vendor

title: Fleet Management for Government Agencies: Accountability and Cost Control
seo_title: Government Fleet Management in Uganda: Accountability
seo_desc: How government fleets in Uganda use tracking and reporting to improve accountability, stop misuse of public vehicles and control fuel and repair costs.
excerpt: Public vehicles are public money. Here is how government agencies use fleet management to prevent misuse, control fuel and maintenance costs and prove accountability.
content:
Government agencies run some of the largest vehicle fleets in East Africa, from ministries and local governments to health, security and infrastructure bodies. Every one of those vehicles is paid for with public money, and the public, auditors and oversight bodies expect it to be used properly. Fleet management gives agencies the tools to show that it is.

Public accountability and audit trails

Government fleets face scrutiny that private fleets do not. Audit queries about vehicle use, fuel and maintenance spending are common, and answering them from paper logbooks is slow and unreliable.

A fleet management system creates an automatic, tamper-resistant audit trail:

  • Every trip recorded, with time, route, distance and duration
  • Driver identification, so each journey is linked to an authorised driver
  • Fuel consumption linked to real journeys
  • Maintenance history with documents, records and invoices
  • Reports ready for internal audit and oversight bodies

Preventing unauthorised use of public vehicles

Misuse of public vehicles, from private errands to weekend trips, is a long-standing challenge. Telematics makes it visible and easier to prevent:

  • After-hours alerts when a vehicle moves outside approved working hours
  • Geofences that flag vehicles leaving their approved area
  • Driver ID that records who is driving, and can block the engine if an unauthorised driver tries to start it
  • Trip history to check that journeys match approved requests

Often, simply knowing that vehicles are tracked changes behaviour.

Fuel and maintenance cost control

Fuel is one of the largest operating costs for any fleet. Telematics data shows:

  • Exactly which vehicles and drivers use the most fuel
  • Which activities and behaviours, such as idling or speeding, contribute to waste
  • Sudden fuel drops that may indicate theft
  • Carbon emissions before and after reduction measures

Maintenance is the other major cost. Electronic reminders based on real mileage, along with engine data such as oil pressure and battery voltage, help keep vehicles in service longer and avoid costly breakdowns and early replacement.

Utilisation and fleet planning

Many government fleets have vehicles that sit idle while others are overused. Utilisation reports show how each vehicle is actually used, helping agencies pool vehicles, plan replacements and avoid buying vehicles they do not need. This is particularly useful when budgets are under pressure.

Revenue authorities and border agencies

For revenue authorities, fleet technology goes further. Electronic cargo tracking helps protect revenue on transit goods, supports faster clearance and enables data sharing with other revenue and border agencies, nationally and regionally. See electronic cargo tracking.

What a procurement process should look for

Public procurement must be transparent and value for money. When preparing tender documents for fleet management, consider specifying:

  • Proven local presence and experience with public sector or large fleets
  • Data ownership and security, including where data is hosted and who can access it
  • Standard reports that match your audit and management requirements
  • Driver ID and after-hours controls
  • Fuel and maintenance modules, not just tracking
  • Training for fleet officers and transport managers
  • Service levels for support and repairs, with local technicians
  • Total cost of ownership over the contract period, not just the unit price

Always follow the applicable public procurement rules and guidelines for your agency.

title: Fleet Management System vs. Spreadsheet: A Real Cost Comparison
seo_title: Fleet Management System vs Spreadsheet: A Real Cost Comparison
seo_desc: What manual, spreadsheet-based fleet tracking really costs compared with a fleet management system, and how to work out your own break-even point.
excerpt: Spreadsheets look free, but manual fleet tracking has hidden costs in fuel, downtime and admin time. Here is how to compare the two honestly for your own fleet.
content:
Many businesses in Uganda and Kenya still run their fleets on spreadsheets, logbooks and phone calls. It works, up to a point, and it seems free. A fleet management system, by contrast, comes with hardware and a monthly fee. So is a system really worth it?

The honest answer depends on your fleet. This article sets out the hidden costs of manual tracking and gives you a simple way to work out your own break-even point.

The hidden costs of manual fleet tracking

A spreadsheet only contains what someone types into it, usually after the fact. That creates costs that never show up as a line item.

Fuel loss you cannot see. Manual records rely on receipts and odometer readings written down by drivers. Siphoning, inflated receipts and unauthorised trips are very hard to detect. If even a small share of your fuel budget is lost, that alone can be more than the cost of a system.

Unauthorised use. Without trip data, you cannot easily see vehicles being used for private errands, side jobs or weekend trips. That means extra fuel, extra wear and extra risk.

Downtime and breakdowns. Services tracked in a spreadsheet are easy to miss. A missed service can turn into a breakdown, a tow, an expensive repair and days off the road, plus a missed delivery or an unhappy client.

Accidents and risky driving. Manual records cannot tell you who speeds, brakes harshly or drives tired. You find out after an accident, when the costs are highest.

Administration time. Someone has to collect logbooks, enter data, chase missing entries and build reports. Count the hours each month and multiply by their cost.

Slow decisions. By the time a monthly spreadsheet is ready, the problems it reveals are weeks old.

What a fleet management system replaces

A system does not just digitise your spreadsheet. It changes how you manage the fleet:

  • Automatic data: location, trips, mileage, hours and fuel recorded without anyone typing
  • Real-time alerts: speeding, unauthorised movement, fuel drops and faults flagged as they happen
  • Ready-made reports: mileage, working hours, fuel and utilisation reports delivered on schedule
  • Maintenance reminders based on actual mileage and engine data
  • Driver scores that make coaching objective

Working out your break-even

Use your own numbers. A simple approach:

Step 1: Estimate your current monthly costs.

  • Fuel spend per month
  • Average maintenance and repair spend per month
  • Hours spent on fleet administration per month, multiplied by staff cost
  • Any recent accident or theft costs, averaged per month

Step 2: Estimate realistic improvements. Be conservative. For example, assume a modest reduction in fuel spend from cutting theft, idling and unauthorised trips, fewer breakdowns, and a few hours of admin time saved each week.

Step 3: Compare with the cost of the system. Add hardware (or the hardware component of the subscription), installation and the monthly fee per vehicle for your whole fleet.

Step 4: Find the break-even. If the estimated monthly savings exceed the monthly cost, the system pays for itself. Many fleets find that fuel savings alone cover the subscription. Run the numbers for your own fleet rather than relying on anyone's headline figure, including ours.

The best way to test your assumptions is to measure a baseline first. Track a few vehicles for a month, compare their real fuel use and trips against your records, and see how big the gap is.

When a spreadsheet is still fine

A system is not always the right answer. A spreadsheet may be enough if:

  • You run only one or two vehicles, used by the owner
  • Vehicles rarely leave town and fuel spend is small
  • There is no theft, misuse or safety concern
  • No client, donor or regulator needs trip or driver reports

As soon as you have several vehicles, drivers you do not supervise directly, or a meaningful fuel bill, the hidden costs usually outweigh the savings.

A middle path

If installing hardware feels like a big step, app-based tracking such as Smartwatch OnTrack tracks vehicles from the driver's phone with no installation. It is a low-cost way to see what your data reveals before committing to a full system.
